note: Round ten: the remaining identity edge cases from my open list: tokens tied to a key, revoke signals, SCIM semantics, rehires, name changes, agency contractors, break-glass accounts, erasure against a hash chain, and clock drift. Expected results written before any code, on 25 Oct 2026. Each case is a small model written for this lab; no real identity provider, real tenant or AI model is tested.

cases.title: Bearer token copied from a log file and replayed from another machine. Asked with a plain bearer token and with a token tied to the caller's own key
cases.expected_in_words: The plain token works for the thief; the key-tied token is refused because the thief cannot sign the request

cases.title: Same, but the thief has taken the caller's key as well as the token (the whole host is compromised)
cases.expected_in_words: The tied token is accepted. This is a limit: tying a token to a key does not help when the key is taken too

cases.title: A person is terminated while their session token has 50 minutes left. Asked with expiry only, and with a revoke signal sent to the app straight away
cases.expected_in_words: Without the signal the token keeps working until it expires; with the signal the app refuses at once

cases.title: A revoke signal arrives that is not signed, then one that is signed by the identity provider
cases.expected_in_words: The unsigned message changes nothing (anyone could send it); the signed one cuts the session

cases.title: Signals arrive out of order: 'access restored' (older) reaches the app after 'access revoked' (newer)
cases.expected_in_words: An app that trusts the last message to arrive switches access back on; an app that orders by event time stays revoked

cases.title: The nightly HR sync replaces a disabled user with a full-record PUT that leaves out the 'active' field, versus a PATCH of only the fields that changed
cases.expected_in_words: The PUT turns the disabled account back on; the PATCH leaves it disabled

cases.title: A person who left comes back after 40 days with the same staff ID. The old account is restored, versus a fresh joiner flow
cases.expected_in_words: The restored account brings back every old entitlement; the fresh flow starts from the new job's baseline only

cases.title: A person changes surname. Accounts are matched by name, versus by an unchanging ID
cases.expected_in_words: Matching by name makes a second account and leaves the old one active; matching by ID updates the one account

cases.title: A contractor from a staffing agency is on the system. The contract ends in the agency's records, which HR never sees. Asked with no end date, and with a required end date of at most 90 days
cases.expected_in_words: With no end date the account is still active after 120 days; with a required end date it is disabled on the day

cases.title: A break-glass account is used at 2 am. Asked with no alert and no password change afterwards, and with an alert within a minute and a new password at check-in
cases.expected_in_words: Without the controls nobody knows and the same password stays valid; with them someone is told and the password no longer works

cases.title: A person asks for their name to be erased from the audit log. Editing the line, versus keeping the name in a separate store under a pseudonym and deleting that
cases.expected_in_words: Editing the line breaks the hash chain from that point; deleting the pseudonym's entry erases the name and the chain still verifies

cases.title: An app's clock runs 15 minutes slow and it is shown a token that expired 10 minutes ago. Asked without and with a check that refuses to decide when the clock is off
cases.expected_in_words: The slow clock accepts the expired token; the app that checks its own clock against a reference refuses
